flashcards.q: What's the minute-by-minute shape of the 45-minute ML/DL depth round?
flashcards.a: 0-5min warmup calibration (fast factual Qs, low scoring weight), 5-20min classical ML depth, 20-38min deep learning depth, 38-45min one open-ended scenario question then close.

flashcards.q: Derive: why does L2 regularization shrink weights but never zero them, while L1 can zero them exactly?
flashcards.a: L2's gradient contribution is proportional to w itself (2*lambda*w) -- it shrinks proportionally but the pull weakens as w approaches zero. L1's subgradient is a constant +/-lambda regardless of magnitude, so once the loss gradient can't counteract that constant pull, it drives small weights exactly to zero.

flashcards.q: Construct the numeric example for why AUC lies under severe class imbalance.
flashcards.a: 10,000 negatives, 100 positives (1% base rate). A model with 95% TPR / 20% FPR still looks decent on AUC, but at that FPR you flag 2,000 negatives to catch 95 positives -- precision ~4.5%. AUC doesn't see this because both axes are rates within their own class.

flashcards.q: PR-AUC of 0.6 -- good or bad? What's the missing context?
flashcards.a: Depends entirely on the base rate: PR-AUC's baseline (random classifier) equals the positive class prevalence. 0.6 against a 0.1% base rate is dramatically better than 0.6 against a 40% base rate. Always anchor to the baseline, never to an absolute number.

flashcards.q: Boosting vs. bagging: what does each reduce, mechanically?
flashcards.a: Bagging (random forest) reduces VARIANCE by averaging many high-variance, low-bias trees trained on random subsets. Boosting reduces BIAS by sequentially fitting each new tree to the residual/negative gradient of the current ensemble.

flashcards.q: Derive the vanishing gradient bound for a sigmoid-activated deep network.
flashcards.a: sigmoid derivative = sigma(z)(1-sigma(z)), maximized at z=0 where it equals 0.25. A 10-layer network's earliest-layer gradient is a product of these factors via the chain rule, bounded by 0.25^10 ~ 1e-6 -- vanishingly small learning signal at the earliest layers.

flashcards.q: ReLU fixes vanishing gradients. What new failure mode does it introduce, and why?
flashcards.a: Dying ReLU: once a unit's weighted input is permanently negative, its gradient is exactly 0 for all future inputs and it never recovers, since both the forward activation and backward gradient are pinned at zero. Fixes: Leaky ReLU, He initialization, lower learning rate, batch norm.

flashcards.q: What's BatchNorm's real mechanism versus its originally claimed mechanism?
flashcards.a: Original claim: reduces 'internal covariate shift.' Challenged by Santurkar et al. 2018, which showed the main benefit is smoothing the loss landscape (reducing the Lipschitz constant), allowing larger stable learning rates -- not the covariate-shift story.

flashcards.q: BatchNorm behaves differently at train vs. inference time -- why, and what's the common bug?
flashcards.a: Train uses per-batch statistics; inference uses a running exponential moving average accumulated during training, since a single inference example has no meaningful batch statistics. Common bug: forgetting to switch the layer to eval mode, causing prediction drift with small inference batches.

flashcards.q: RNN vs CNN vs Transformer: state the path-length and compute tradeoff for each.
flashcards.a: RNN: O(n) sequential steps, O(n) path length between distant tokens, no parallelization. CNN (dilated): parallelizable, O(log n) path length. Transformer: O(1) path length via full self-attention, fully parallelizable, but O(n^2) time/memory in sequence length.

flashcards.q: Derive the softmax+cross-entropy gradient simplification, and name the numerical stability fix.
flashcards.a: Gradient w.r.t. logits simplifies to (p_i - y_i) -- a remarkably clean result, which is why the pairing is standard. Naive exponentiation overflows on large logits; fix is the log-sum-exp trick, subtracting max(z) before exponentiating (mathematically identical, numerically stable).

flashcards.q: Why does a supervised ranker trained on logged clicks have a structural blind spot for new content?
flashcards.a: It only ever sees outcomes for items the previous policy chose to show -- an off-policy bias problem, not a lack of cleverness. It can never learn that an unshown item might have been better. A contextual bandit explicitly allocates traffic to exploration to fix this.

flashcards.q: Inverted dropout: what's the scaling correction, applied when, and what bug results from forgetting it?
flashcards.a: Scale activations by 1/(1-p) during TRAINING (inverted dropout) so inference needs no special-casing. Forgetting the correction, or forgetting to disable dropout at eval time, causes an inexplicably higher validation loss than training loss beyond normal generalization gap.

flashcards.q: F1 score assumes what, and when does that assumption fail?
flashcards.a: F1 (harmonic mean of precision/recall) implicitly assumes equal business cost for false positives and false negatives -- rarely true. Use F-beta with beta chosen from the real cost ratio instead (beta=2 weights recall twice as important, e.g. for cancer screening or fraud).

flashcards.q: What's the ML/DL round's calibration rule for a definition-only answer, even if accurate?
flashcards.a: A definition alone scores no better than a 2/5 on Correctness/depth, because a definition is not a derivation -- the round is calibrated to require mechanism, not vocabulary.
